newsitem.title: CHINA: Clinton decision on China trade status hailed.
newsitem.headline: Clinton decision on China trade status hailed.

text.p: China on Tuesday hailed U.S. President Bill Clinton's decision to renew its most favoured trading status but urged Washington to grant the trade concessions on a permanent basis.
Clinton's move also drew praise in Taiwan and Hong Kong, whose economies are closely tied to China.

"We welcome President Clinton's announcement to extend Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status for China," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing. "We think this decision by President Clinton is a wise decision."

Clinton told U.S. businessmen on Monday he planned to renew most favoured nation trade status for China for another year, firing the opening shot in what is expected to be a new foreign policy battle with Congress.
The U.S. president said he had decided to grant China what amounts to normal trade tariff status for the next year despite disputes with Beijing on many issues, notably human rights.
But Shen said the annual review of the trading status for China was not conducive to the normal and stable development of trade ties, and urged Washington to grant permanent MFN.
Shen also fired a shot at the U.S. Congress, where opponents of trade concessions to China are expected to mount the fiercest congressional battle in years to overturn Clinton's decision.
"The U.S. Congress should not engage in unnecessary interference in MFN for China or cancel MFN," Shen said. "This is not in the interests of either side."
In Hong Kong, the decision was seen as particularly important as the British colony prepares for its return to Chinese rule on July 1.
"The chamber is very happy," Erica Ng, assistant manager of international affairs at the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, told Reuters.
"If (MFN) is not renewed, it will affect Hong Kong economically and greatly affect confidence in the territory," she said.
China accounts for much of the colony's re-export trade and a withdrawal of MFN could mean the loss of up to US$30 billion annually in trade and related industry revenues.
Gross domestic product growth could be cut by about three percentage points and some 86,000 jobs in Hong Kong could be at risk, according to some estimates.
China's rival Taiwan also had praise for the American president and expressed hope that Congress would back his decision.
"This is a very good development for Taiwan businessmen investing in the mainland," Chen Ruey-long, deputy director of the cabinet's Board of Foreign Trade, said on state radio.
"Mainland China's MFN status will help Taiwan businessmen expand in the U.S. market," Chen said.
Some 30,000 Taiwanese firms have poured more than US$30 billion in investments into the mainland despite a bitter rivalry dating to the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
The United States is the main market for many Taiwan-funded companies operating in China.

The United States also has an interest in maintaining normal trade relations. U.S. officials estimate that 170,000 U.S. jobs depend on exports to China and that ending MFN could cost U.S. consumers $600 million a year in higher prices for shoes, clothing and appliances.

U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said this year's decision would be closer than last year's 286-141 vote in the House to back Clinton on MFN. But advocates and even opponents expect the president's policy ultimately to survive.
